Symmachus
sĭm´a-kŭs
n. (Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, c. 345–402, pagan senator and prefect of Rome, who pleaded in 384 for the restoration of the Altar of Victory and recommended Augustine for the chair of rhetoric at Milan)
Greek summachos, ally, fellow-fighter. Not to be confused with Symmachus the second-century translator of the Old Testament, or the later Pope Symmachus.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Symmachus was the most eloquent pagan of his generation and the leader of the senators who held to the old gods. When the emperor Gratian removed the Altar of Victory from the senate house, Symmachus, as prefect of the city, petitioned the young Valentinian II in 384 to restore it. His plea became famous for one sentence: that not by one road only can men come to so great a mystery. Ambrose answered him in two letters, and the altar was not restored. The gospel's answer is Christ's: “I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me” (Joh 14:6), and Peter's: “Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved” (Act 4:12). The first commandment had settled it at Sinai: “Thou shalt have no other gods before me” (Exo 20:3). In the same year Symmachus chose the young African Augustine, then still a Manichee, for the post of rhetor at Milan, and so sent him, without knowing it, to sit under Ambrose. Elijah's question hung over his whole career: “How long halt ye between two opinions?” (1Ki 18:21).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines plurality as a number consisting of two or more of the same kind; and, in the church, the holding of two or more benefices by one clergyman.

PLURALITY, n. A number consisting of two or more of the same kind.

2. A state of being or having a greater number.

3. In the church, the holding of two or more benefices by the same clergyman.

Key Scripture

Joh 14:6 — "Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me."

Act 4:12 — "Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved."

Exo 20:3 — "Thou shalt have no other gods before me."

1Ki 18:21 — "And Elijah came unto all the people, and said, How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him. And the people answered him not a word."

Modern Corruption

‘Not by one road’ is the creed of religious pluralism, and Symmachus stated it more gracefully in 384 than any modern interfaith declaration has managed.

expand to see more

Symmachus's argument has every modern note: the antiquity of the traditions, respect for the ancestors, the mystery too great for any one path, and the request for public space for all religions. It is now the default of Western culture and the working assumption of much liberal Christianity, which treats Christ as one way among many to a divine mystery. It sounds humble. It is a denial that God has spoken.

Ambrose's answer was that Christians cannot sanction an altar to a false god in the place where they are called to serve the true one; the gospel's exclusive claim is not arrogance but the content of the message. The providence in the story is the other half of the recovery. The man who pleaded for many roads sent Augustine down the one road that leads to the Father.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek hodos (G3598), way, road; Hebrew pasach (H6452), to halt, limp; Greek soteria (G4991), salvation.

Hebrew pasach (H6452) — to limp, halt; 1 Kings 18:21, 26.

Usage

"“no man cometh unto the Father, but by me” (Joh 14:6) — the answer to ‘not by one road.’"

"“none other name under heaven” (Act 4:12) — the exclusive gospel."

"“How long halt ye between two opinions?” (1Ki 18:21) — Elijah to every Symmachus."
